eras.note: Britain and the Congo Free State divided the Luapula valley in 1894. British forces burned Mwata Kazembe X's capital in 1899 after he resisted tax collection, and he later returned and rebuilt at Mwansabombwe.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company

eras.note: The chieftainship continued after independence, and the Mutomboko festival, held at the end of July, began in 1971.

regions.label: Northern and Muchinga — Bemba country
regions.sub: Kasama, Mbala, Mpika, Chinsali, Mpulungu, Nakonde

eras.note: Before registers. The Bemba entered Zambia before 1740 and expanded by conquest in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, displacing the Lungu, Mambwe and Bisa.

eras.polity: British South Africa Company sphere; North-Eastern Rhodesia from 1900
eras.note: Rhodes obtained mineral concessions in 1888; North-Eastern Rhodesia was created by Order in Council in January 1900.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company

eras.note: Under the protectorate the Chitimukulu's role became more ceremonial than executive, and many Bemba moved to the Copperbelt in the 1930s for mining work.

regions.label: Liberia - Montserrado and the settler coast
regions.sub: Monrovia, Buchanan, Robertsport, Greenville, Harbel

eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese explorers made contact in 1462 and called it the Pepper Coast; the Dutch set up and abandoned trading posts in 1602 and 1663.

The American Colonization Society acquired Cape Mesurado, near Monrovia, in 1821. The Society's own records, including letters from Liberia for 1833-1917, passenger lists and land grants, are held by the Library of Congress and are largely un-indexed; they are the main source for the first settlers. Mississippi-in-Africa was settled at Sinoe in 1835 as a separate colony.

Separate colonies merged into the Commonwealth of Liberia, dated 1838 or 1839 depending on the source, with Monrovia as capital. Mississippi-in-Africa was annexed by Liberia in 1842. Montserrado and Grand Bassa counties date from 1839.

Independence was declared on 26 July 1847. Sinoe County dates from 1843 or 1847 and Grand Cape Mount from 1844, depending on the source. FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018; births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and marriage registers go to the Center for National Documents and Records in Monrovia.

eras.polity: Liberia - coup, civil wars and new counties
eras.note: Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. The first civil war began in December 1989 and the second ran 1999-2003. Bomi County was created in 1984, Margibi and Rivercess in 1985.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003 and UNMIL took over peacekeeping on 1 October 2003.

regions.label: Liberia - Maryland in Africa and the south-east
regions.sub: Harper (Cape Palmas), Pleebo, Barclayville, Fish Town, Zwedru

eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese contact dates from 1462.

The Maryland legislature funded the emigration of free Black Americans and former slaves in 1831, and settlement at Cape Palmas began on 12 February 1834 as Maryland in Africa. The colony was funded by the Maryland legislature, not by the American Colonization Society.

eras.polity: State of Maryland - an independent republic from 1854
eras.note: The colony declared statehood as the State of Maryland on 2 February 1841 and independence as Maryland in Liberia on 29 May 1854. The date it joined Liberia is 1857 on the Maryland page (18 March or 6 April depending on the passage) and 1854 on the general history of Liberia.

Maryland became a county of Liberia in 1857, and Grand Gedeh, formerly part of the interior provinces, became a county in 1964. Births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018.

eras.polity: Liberia - coup, civil wars and new counties
eras.note: Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. Grand Kru County was created in 1984 and River Gee in 2000. The first civil war began in December 1989 and the second ran 1999-2003.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003.

regions.label: Liberia - Lofa, Bong, Nimba and the interior
regions.sub: Gbarnga, Voinjama, Sanniquellie, Ganta, Kakata

eras.polity: Interior of the Pepper Coast - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. The American Colonization Society settlements of 1821-1847 lay on the coast.

eras.polity: Republic of Liberia - Central, Western and Eastern Provinces
eras.note: This ground was administered as the Central, Western and Eastern Provinces, not as counties, until 1964. A League of Nations report of 1930 criticised the government's treatment of indigenous people, and indigenous Liberians gained the vote in 1951.

eras.polity: Republic of Liberia - Lofa, Bong and Nimba counties
eras.note: Bong, Lofa, Nimba and Grand Gedeh were made counties in 1964. Births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018.

Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. The First Liberian Civil War began in December 1989, with Charles Taylor's forces invading from Cote d'Ivoire, and the second war ran 1999-2003. Gbarpolu County was created in 2001.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003.

regions.label: Sierra Leone - the Colony and the Protectorate
regions.sub: Freetown, Bo, Kenema, Makeni, Bonthe

eras.note: Before registers.

About 400 formerly enslaved Black Britons arrived on 15 May 1787 and settled Granville Town on land bought from King Tom and the regent Naimbanna II. King Jemmy burned it in 1789 and settlers regathered near Fourah Bay in 1791.

Nova Scotian settlers arrived in February-March 1792 and Freetown was named on 11 March. More than 500 Jamaican Maroons arrived in 1800, and their Maroon Town was founded on the land of the suppressed Nova Scotian rebels.

eras.polity: Crown Colony of Sierra Leone - Freetown and the Liberated Africans
eras.note: The Colony was a Crown colony from 1808 and the base of the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron, whose rescued captives were called Liberated Africans or Recaptives. The Sierra Leone Public Archives in Freetown hold nineteenth-century Liberated African Department registers, including a series labelled 1808-1845, which have been scanned by the British Library's Endangered Archives Programme.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Sierra Leone
eras.note: A proclamation of 31 August 1896 declared the surrounding country a British Protectorate. The Colony stayed a separate political entity and the Protectorate was governed from it until the 1950s; the Hut Tax War of 1898 was fought in the Protectorate. The Colony and the Protectorate therefore have different legal and record histories.
Independence came on 27 April 1961. Today's divisions are the Eastern, Northern, North West, Southern and Western Area provinces.

regions.label: Ghana - Ashanti, Ahafo, Bono and the Western North
regions.sub: Kumasi, Sunyani, Techiman, Bibiani, Goaso

eras.note: Before registers.
Asante gained independence from Denkyira in 1701 and the Asante Union was founded; Bono was conquered in 1722. The first Anglo-Ashanti war was in 1823-24 and the second in 1863-64.

Britain burned Kumasi in the war of 1873-74 and the Asantehene signed a treaty in July 1874. The Gold Coast Colony was formally established on the coast on 24 July 1874, but Asante remained outside it.

eras.polity: Asante annexed - protectorate and the War of the Golden Stool
eras.note: Britain annexed Asante in January 1896 and proclaimed a protectorate; the War of the Golden Stool followed in March-September 1900.

eras.polity: Ashanti Colony, part of the Gold Coast
eras.note: The Ashanti Crown Colony was created on 26 September 1901 and joined the Gold Coast on 1 January 1902; some pages date this to 1901 and others to 1902. The Asante Confederacy was restored under colonial rule in 1935. The National Archives of Ghana in Accra holds births, marriages and deaths for Europeans and Africans from 1872.

Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957. In 2018 several new regions were created by splitting the Northern, Volta, Western and Brong-Ahafo regions; older records may sit under the former, larger region.

regions.label: Ghana - Volta and Oti, the Trans-Volta Togoland
regions.sub: Ho, Hohoe, Kpando, Nkwanta, Kete Krachi

eras.polity: Ewe, Guan and other states - before registers
eras.note: Before registers.
Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty with chief Mlapa III on 5 July 1884 and declared a German protectorate on the Slave Coast. The Reichskolonialamt files on Togo are in the Bundesarchiv (R 1001).

eras.polity: Anglo-French occupation and the British zone
eras.note: Anglo-French forces invaded in August 1914 and Togoland surrendered on 26 August 1914. On 27 December 1916 it was divided into British and French zones, and the British zone was run as part of the Gold Coast under the name Trans-Volta Togo.

eras.polity: British Togoland under League of Nations mandate
eras.note: Britain received a Class B mandate on 20 July 1922. The territory was administered as part of the Gold Coast.

The territory became a UN Trust Territory under British administration on 13 December 1946. A plebiscite on 9 May 1956 returned about 58 percent for integration with the Gold Coast, and it was annexed to Ghana on 6 March 1957 under the Ghana Independence Act.

Ho, the capital of British Togoland, is now the capital of the Volta Region, which includes much of the former mandate territory. In 2018 the Volta Region was one of four regions split to create new regions.

regions.label: Ghana - the Northern Territories
regions.sub: Tamale, Wa, Bolgatanga, Bawku, Damongo

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Dagomba, Mamprusi, Gonja and Wa states
eras.note: Dagomba was conquered by Asante in the early 1770s and began paying annual tribute.

eras.polity: British treaties and the Northern Territories district
eras.note: British treaties of 1896 with the chiefs of Bona, Dagarti, Wa and Mamprusi barred them from dealings with other powers. The area became a district in 1897.

A 1901 Order in Council made it a protectorate, dated 1 January 1902 or 1901 depending on the source. It was run by the Governor of the Gold Coast through a Chief Commissioner at Gambaga. The National Archives of Ghana in Accra holds births, marriages and deaths from 1872.
The territories joined Ghana on 6 March 1957. In 2018 the Northern Region was among four regions split to create new ones; a place's older records may sit under the former, larger region.

regions.label: Namibia - Windhoek, Walvis Bay and the central regions
regions.sub: Windhoek, Swakopmund, Walvis Bay, Gobabis, Otjiwarongo

eras.polity: Nama, Herero and Damara - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Herero herders moved into this country in the seventeenth century and missionaries arrived in the early 1800s.

eras.polity: Walvis Bay annexed to the Cape; Herero and Nama land inland
eras.note: Britain took Walvis Bay in 1878 (some sources give 1884). Inland the country remained Herero and Nama land.

Germany claimed the territory in 1884 after Adolf Lüderitz bought land at Angra Pequena. German forces carried out the Herero and Nama genocide in 1904-08. The Red Line of 1896, first a rinderpest cordon, became a political boundary in 1907, and police protection was limited to the areas where German economic interests were concentrated. The National Archives of Namibia in Windhoek hold the German colonial government records and the Bundesarchiv holds the Reichskolonialamt files; FamilySearch lists civil registration of marriages 1893-1930 and deaths 1894-1954 for South West Africa.
South African forces occupied the territory in 1915.

eras.polity: South West Africa under South African mandate
eras.note: South Africa governed under a League of Nations mandate from 1920, and the UN General Assembly ended the mandate in 1966. The Dutch Reformed Church registers of Namibia, 1904-2010, are on FamilySearch; the Windhoek archives hold South African administration records. Walvis Bay remained South African.

eras.polity: Independent Namibia; Walvis Bay still South African
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990, but Walvis Bay was transferred from South Africa only in 1994.

eras.polity: Namibia - Erongo, Khomas, Hardap, Omaheke and Otjozondjupa
eras.note: Walvis Bay was transferred to Namibia in 1994. The National Archives of Namibia is governed by the Archives Act 12 of 1992.

regions.label: Namibia - Ovamboland and the Kunene
regions.sub: Oshakati, Ondangwa, Opuwo, Ruacana, Outapi

eras.polity: Ovambo kingdoms and Herero herders - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Ovambo and Kavango farmers lived in the north, and Finnish Lutheran missionaries began work in Ovamboland in the 1870s.

eras.polity: German South West Africa - north of the Red Line
eras.note: The Red Line became a political boundary in 1907, and Oshana, Omusati and Kunene are among the regions listed north of it; the northern areas were largely governed indirectly through traditional authorities.

South Africa occupied the territory in 1915 and governed it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920. Finnish Lutheran missionaries were active from the 1870s and the Ovambo-Kavango Evangelical Lutheran Church was formed in 1954.

Ovamboland was set up as a Bantustan in 1968 under the Odendaal Plan and gained self-government in 1973. A Representative Authority replaced the Bantustan in 1980 and Ovamboland was abolished in May 1989.

eras.polity: Namibia - Kunene, Omusati, Oshana, Ohangwena and Oshikoto
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. The National Archives of Namibia in Windhoek hold records of the German and South African administrations.

regions.label: Namibia - Kavango and the Caprivi Strip
regions.sub: Rundu, Nkurenkuru, Katima Mulilo, Divundu

eras.polity: Kavango and Zambezi river peoples - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Ovambo and Kavango farmers lived in the north of what is now Namibia.

eras.polity: German South West Africa - the Caprivi Strip and Kavango
eras.note: Germany acquired the Caprivi Strip through the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty with Britain in 1890, mainly for access to the Zambezi. The Kavango and Zambezi lay north of the Red Line, where rule was largely indirect through traditional authorities.

South Africa occupied the territory in 1915 and held it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920. The Ovambo-Kavango Evangelical Lutheran Church was formed in 1954. FamilySearch lists church records for Katima Mulilo.
South Africa created the Eastern Caprivi homeland in 1976 and transferred its administration to the South West African government in 1980.

eras.polity: Namibia - Kavango East, Kavango West and Zambezi
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. In 1999 the International Court of Justice ruled that Kasikili/Sedudu Island belongs to Botswana.

regions.label: The Orange River borderland - Colesberg and Philippolis
regions.sub: Colesberg, Philippolis, Norvalspont

eras.polity: Griqua mission territory at Philippolis; Cape Colony at Colesberg
eras.note: The London Missionary Society founded Philippolis in 1823 for the Griqua, and Adam Kok II moved there in 1826. Colesberg was founded in 1830 and named for a governor of the Cape Colony.

eras.polity: Orange River Sovereignty north of the river
eras.note: Harry Smith proclaimed British sovereignty over the country between the Orange and Vaal rivers on 3 February 1848, with Bloemfontein as the capital.

eras.polity: Orange Free State; Cape Colony south of the river
eras.note: Britain renounced the Sovereignty and the Orange River Convention of 23 February 1854 recognised the Orange Free State. Britain annexed the diamond fields as Griqualand West in 1871, and the Cape gained responsible government in 1872. Orange Free State marriages are registered from 1848 and births and deaths from 1903; Cape births and deaths from 1895.

eras.polity: Orange River Colony and Cape Colony
eras.note: Britain annexed the Orange Free State as the Orange River Colony in 1900 and the Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 ended the republic's independence.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province and Orange Free State
eras.note: The Cape Colony and the Orange River Colony joined the Union in 1910, as the Cape Province and the Orange Free State province. Home Affairs civil registers have not been transferred to the National Archives.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Northern Cape and Free State
eras.note: Colesberg is now in the Northern Cape and Philippolis in the Free State, on opposite sides of the old Cape-Free State line.

regions.label: The Stormberg and the north-eastern Cape - Burgersdorp, Barkly East
regions.sub: Burgersdorp, Barkly East, Dordrecht, Lady Grey, Indwe

eras.note: Before registers.
The Anglo-Dutch treaty of 1814 confirmed British possession of the Cape, which Britain had re-occupied in 1806.

eras.polity: Cape Colony - Burgersdorp and the Stormberg
eras.note: Burgersdorp was established in 1846. Cape marriage registration is dated from 1700, with Dutch Reformed Church records preceding civil registration and matrimonial court records filling gaps where parish registers are missing.
The Cape gained responsible government in 1872. Civil registration of births and deaths in the Cape began in 1895.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Colony joined the Union in 1910 as the Cape Province. Home Affairs civil registers are held by Home Affairs, not by the National Archives.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Eastern Cape
eras.note: Burgersdorp lies in the Joe Gqabi District.

regions.label: British Kaffraria and the Border - East London, Stutterheim
regions.sub: East London, King William's Town, Stutterheim, Bhisho

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Queen Adelaide Province and Queen Adelaide Land
eras.note: Governor D'Urban annexed the area as Queen Adelaide Province in 1835 and London disapproved; it was disannexed and renamed the Queen Adelaide Land district, with Grahamstown as its capital, and indigenous rule largely returned.

Harry Smith annexed the territory as the British Kaffraria Colony in 1847, with King William's Town as capital, and it became a separate Crown Colony in 1860. German emigrants arrived in 1858-59 and 1877-78.
British Kaffraria was incorporated into the Cape Colony on 17 April 1866. Cape civil registration of births and deaths began in 1895.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Colony joined the Union in 1910.
The area formed the basis of the Ciskei homeland, self-governing from 1972 and nominally independent from 4 December 1981, a status not recognised internationally. Its capital was Bisho.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Eastern Cape
eras.note: Ciskei was reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994.

regimeNote: Five of these carry a Wikidata id and the dates Wikidata holds for them. The rest do not, and that is deliberate: fuzzy matching offered Circassia for Croatia, Audhali for Australia and Basutoland for Poland, and several of the labels here — «Aquileia · Gorizia · Frankopan», «German occupation» — are this project's own shorthand for a situation rather than the name of a state. An honest blank beats a plausible lie. data/polities-wikidata.json holds 1,857 former countries with dates as a REFERENCE for whoever authors the next region, not as something a machine should match automatically.
regimeArchivesNote: `archives` is WHICH MODERN STATE HELD THIS GROUND under that regime — the country whose flag flew over it, and whose archive inherited the paper. Habsburg is AT and HU because the Dual Monarchy filed in both capitals; Galicia is PL and UA because the border of 1945 cut it and its archives in half. It is NOT a claim about who owns the ground today, and it is not a border: it is the answer to «whose archive do I write to for these years, and whose flag was over the parish when the entry was made». A regime that left no single successor state — the Aquileia/Gorizia/Frankopan feudal centuries — carries an empty list on purpose, because a guess at which modern capital inherited a patriarchate is exactly the inference this atlas refuses elsewhere. Read by abroadFor() for the «also governed from» sources, and by eraFlagsHtml() for the flags over the selected era.
countriesNote: Derived from each ring — the vertices, the edge midpoints and the centre — rather than from the places walked inside it. A region is a piece of ground and which countries it covers is a fact about the ground, not about whether anybody has walked a parish in it yet. A country claimed by a single sampled point is dropped as a corner clipping a neighbour.
